name: LifeWire MuteSpeak Subvocal Communicator
body_location: laryngeal/submental — sensor array along the larynx and floor of mouth
description:
The MuteSpeak captures the neuromuscular signals that precede audible speech — the micro-contractions of the tongue, soft palate, and laryngeal musculature that occur a fraction of a second before sound is produced — and converts them into a clear digital voice signal transmitted via short-range Bluetooth-equivalent mesh to paired devices, earpieces, or contacts. No sound is produced at the lips. The implant uses a shallow-mount flexible sensor ribbon sutured beneath the jaw and a secondary node at the thyroid cartilage, both connected to a subcutaneous signal processor no larger than a thumbnail seated behind the ear. Voice profiles are personalized during a two-week calibration period, during which the user speaks normally to train the system's phoneme-mapping algorithm. After calibration, transmission fidelity reaches roughly 96% accuracy for the user's native language and up to 88% for learned secondary languages.

The MuteSpeak is ubiquitous across Tier 2 and 3 life in GLMZ. Office workers use it to take calls during meetings without leaving the room. Parents whisper instructions to their kids across a noisy market without anyone nearby noticing. Teenagers use it to talk to friends during class, a fact every school administrator in the city has made peace with. For people in service industries — warehouse floors, loud kitchens, transit hubs — it replaces shouting entirely. Paired with an in-ear receiver implant or a standard consumer earpiece, two people can have a full conversation in a crowded room with their faces blank and still. The effect, to outsiders, is slightly uncanny — two people standing together, motionless, apparently thinking.
installation_requirements: Outpatient clinic or licensed pharmacy implant kiosk; local anesthetic only; 45-minute procedure; two-week calibration period post-installation
maintenance: Annual firmware update recommended; sensor ribbon replacement every 4-5 years; no battery — passive power draw from body heat via thermoelectric cell

side_effects: Mild throat tightness during the first week of calibration
Occasional phantom transmission — system misreads swallowing or yawning as speech during early calibration
Some users report a persistent low awareness of their own jaw muscles, described as 'feeling like you're always about to talk'
Rare: minor skin irritation at sensor ribbon site during humidity spikes
cultural_context: The MuteSpeak has been on the market long enough — nearly two decades — that it no longer reads as unusual. In Tier 2 and 3 spaces, it is as unremarkable as a contact lens. The tell is subtle: people who use it tend to go very still when they're on a call, eyes slightly unfocused, jaw relaxed. Longtime users sometimes develop the habit of going still even when speaking normally, having trained themselves not to move. In Tier 1 Shelf communities, cheaper gray-market variants — called 'hushmods' — circulate with lower fidelity and no calibration support, producing the clipped, slightly robotic transmissions that gave rise to the slang term 'ghostalk.' There is a small but vocal cultural contingent, mostly older Tier 3 adults, who find the technology socially alienating — they argue that removing audible speech from a room changes the emotional register of shared space. Most people under 35 consider this opinion quaint.
known_users: Office workers and corporate employees who take calls in open-plan environments
Parents of young children managing logistics in public spaces
Transit and warehouse workers in high-noise environments
Teenagers and young adults using it for private conversation in shared spaces
People with social anxiety who find silent communication lower-stakes
Service industry workers coordinating across loud floors
story_hooks: A player character overhears — via a hacked MuteSpeak channel — a conversation between two people standing silently in a crowd, and realizes they are discussing something that directly implicates the party.
A witness to a crime insists they saw nothing and heard nothing — but a MuteSpeak log recovered from the scene contains a full transcript of what they transmitted to someone during the event.

A gray-market 'hushmod' variant being sold in Tier 1 has a hidden listener function that forwards all subvocal transmissions to an unknown third party — and someone in the party's network just got one installed.
